newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Michigan roads crumbling under pothole epidemic.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Michigan roads crumbling under pothole epidemic.

text.p: Here in Motor City, where the Big Three automakers spend billions of dollars to supply America with new cars and trucks, a great irony confronts drivers every time they get behind the wheel.
The cars may be fine but the roads are crumbling under an epidemic of rim-bending potholes.

Spring potholes, of course, are a fact of life in northern cities. As frozen moisture under the road thaws, it leaves an empty space between soil and pavement. Vehicles driving over the cavity break apart the surface and a pothole is born.
But drivers in Michigan and its largest city, who already clatter over some of the worst roads in the country, are facing a chuckhole crisis of record proportions this year.
How bad are the roads?

Patricia Thornhill of Detroit sent this reply to the Detroit Free Press after the newspaper solicited pothole horror stories this spring: "My favorite pothole is so deep that I have to wear a sports bra just to drive down the street."

One mid-state highway is now so rutted that John Niemela, director of the County Road Association, which represents Michigan's 83 county road commissions, was forced to change his commute to work in Lansing, the state capitol.
"The roads I've driven on historically are probably worse this year than I've ever seen them," he said, echoing a comment heard more and more around the state.

In the 1950s, Michigan roads were regarded as the best in the country, he said. But decades of inattention and underfunding are taking a toll. Now, about 29 percent of Michigan's 117,000 miles (188,000 km) of roads are rated poor and two-thirds are either poor or fair. The remaining one-third have a good rating.
ROADS GET WORSE FASTER
Unfortunately, the worse a road is, the faster it will fall further into disprepair, Niemela said. "As they get worse, they get worse faster."

AAA Michigan, the state's largest auto insurance carrier, normally gets between 10,000 and 15,000 pothole claims a year. Preliminary indications from this spring point to a record number of claims for 1997, spokeswoman Nancy Cain said.

AAA was getting so many pothole reports that it started a pothole hotline and began distributing a list of Michigan's top 10 worst roads. In its first week of operation the hotine received more than 300 calls.

And for the first time ever, potholes are becoming a potent political issue, said Ed Sarpolus, vice president of EPIC/MRI, a Lansing-based polling firm. In an unprecedented action, traditionally anti-tax business groups are joining local governments in a unified plea for Gov. John Engler to raise the state's fuel tax, which has not gone up since 1984.

"Except for the governor there is now becoming one voice," Sarpolis said. "The Grand Rapids chamber, the Detroit chamber, the mayors, the townships, the county organizations and road builders are all singing from the same sheet of music."
GOVERNOR SUFFERS POTHOLE BACKLASH

Engler, a Republican, has gained national attention for slashing taxes 21 times and saving $6.5 billion since he took office in 1991, but his reluctance to raise the tax on motor fuel means he is now bearing the brunt of public anger. Democratic state legislators are sporting buttons with Engler's photo that say, "Pothole John. Pave Over Engler in '98."

In his January state of the state address, Engler reaffirmed his opposition to a tax hike and put forward a seven-point plan of his own to reform and wring more efficiencies out of the current system.

As one example, state officials will cut $100 million out of the Michigan Department of Transportation budget this fiscal year, Engler spokesman John Truscott said. "Raising the gas tax would be the easy way out, but it doesn't fix some of the problems in the system," he said.

Meantime, the potholes get bigger for Michigan drivers, and they are getting more expensive. The usual damage of bent rims and flat tires is giving way to more costly repairs -- sometimes several thousand dollars -- because of the more sophisticated suspensions and anti-lock brake systems now found on cars.
